fields.foundation: The Chagatai Khanate was allotted rather than founded. It was a territorial appanage (ulus) that Genghis Khan assigned to his second son Chagatai when he divided the Mongol Empire's conquests, and this inherited subordination marked the khanate for much of its existence. Chagatai Khan (r. 1227–1242) received lands formerly belonging to the Qara Khitai and the Khwarazmian realm: Transoxiana (much of modern Uzbekistan), the Ili River valley, Kashgaria and the Tarim Basin, and the Semirechye steppe. The domain included the great Silk Road cities of Samarkand and Bukhara as well as the broad pastoral grasslands of the Central Asian steppe. The tension between urban commercial civilisation and nomadic pastoral tradition was present in the khanate from the start. Chagatai himself was a strict guardian of Mongol tradition. He enforced the Yasa (Mongol customary law) rigorously and was remembered by Muslim chroniclers as hostile to Islamic practice, reportedly forbidding the ritual slaughter of animals and ablution in running water in accordance with Mongol custom. During Chagatai's lifetime the khanate was plainly subordinate to the Great Khan in Karakorum. The sedentary cities of Transoxiana were administered by Mahmud Yalavach and later his son Mas'ud Beg, Khwarazmian Muslims answerable to the Great Khan rather than to Chagatai, and the khanate had no independent foreign policy, little revenue base beyond the nomadic pastures, and limited capacity to act without the Great Khan's sanction. For its first three decades it was therefore a subordinate domain within the Mongol imperial system, whose ruler's main task was to keep order among the nomads of his pastures and provide contingents for the Great Khan's campaigns. That changed when Alghu (r. 1260–1266) used the civil war between Kublai and Ariq Böke to assert real independence.
fields.socioeconomy: The Chagatai Khanate's economy rested on the Silk Road, the web of overland routes linking China to the Mediterranean that passed through the khanate's Central Asian heartland, and one of the most important commercial networks of the pre-modern world. The cities of Transoxiana, Samarkand, Bukhara and the smaller commercial centres along the Zerafshan and Amu Darya rivers, had been among the most prosperous urban centres in the world for centuries before the Mongol conquest. Despite the devastation of the Mongol invasion of Central Asia in 1219–1221, they recovered over time under Mongol protection of long-distance trade. During the Pax Mongolica of the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries, Mongol guarantees of safe conduct allowed merchants to travel across Eurasia on a scale not seen before. The khanate benefited through tolls and taxes on goods passing through its territory, although its frequent wars with the Yuan and the Ilkhanate repeatedly disrupted the routes. Kebek Khan's monetary reform of around 1321 introduced a standardised silver coinage so widely trusted that the coins became known as kebeks. It was the most significant Chagatai contribution to the commercial infrastructure of Central Asia. The khanate's persistent economic problem was the conflict between its nomadic aristocracy, whose wealth came from herds, war booty and tribute from subject sedentary populations, and the urban merchant class, which required stable government, predictable taxation and secure property. Tarmashirin's shift of the political centre towards Transoxiana in the early 1330s was an attempt to settle the matter in favour of the sedentary economy, but it alienated the eastern nomadic tribes on whose military power Chagataid authority finally rested. Timur's rise to power in Transoxiana in the 1360s, completed by 1370, transferred the great commercial cities to a more effectively sedentary regime and ended the Chagataid hold on its richest inheritance.
fields.military: The Chagatai military was built on the Mongol tradition of mounted archery: unmatched mobility, the firepower of the composite bow, feigned retreats and calculated terror. With these the original Mongol armies had conquered peoples from China to Poland. The khanate used this tradition most effectively during the dominance of Kaidu (d. 1301). The combined forces of Kaidu's Ögedeid domains and the Chagatai khan Duwa (r. 1282–1307), whom Kaidu had installed, then waged sustained war against the Yuan dynasty of Kublai Khan and his successors in Central Asia, raiding the Uyghur lands and Mongolia and keeping pressure on the Yuan frontier for nearly three decades. Chagataid armies also crossed the Hindu Kush to invade the Delhi Sultanate repeatedly from the 1290s, under commanders sent by Duwa such as his son Qutlugh Khwaja, who led a great army to the outskirts of Delhi in 1299. Alauddin Khalji's strong forces turned back these invasions and prevented any permanent Mongol occupation of northern India. A raid into India under Tarmashirin in the late 1320s, reportedly reaching deep into the Punjab towards Delhi, was a late display of force, but it was a plundering expedition rather than a conquest and left the khanate's strategic position unchanged. The khanate's basic military weakness was its limited capacity for siege warfare. Mongol cavalry was devastating in open country but struggled against strongly fortified cities of the kind that defended both Yuan and Indian territories. As the khanate fragmented after 1334, military power was dispersed among competing tribal confederations, each able to raid but none capable of coordinated strategic action on the scale the khanate had briefly achieved.
fields.governance: The Chagatai Khanate's government was always contested between the Genghisid legitimacy of the Chagataid khans and the practical power of the great tribal groupings, among them the Dughlat in the east and the Barlas, Jalayir and Qara'una in the west. Their military strength made them the khanate's effective rulers whenever a khan lacked the personal authority to enforce his will. The Genghisid principle, that only male-line descendants of Genghis Khan could hold the title of khan, was the dynasty's greatest asset and also a severe constraint, since the Chagataid line could not be replaced even by more effective rulers. Timur (Tamerlane), the most powerful ruler of the late fourteenth-century Islamic world, therefore governed through puppet Chagataid khans such as Soyurghatmish rather than taking the title himself, and styled himself güregen, “royal son-in-law”, through his marriage to a Genghisid princess. The khanate's legal framework drew on the Yasa, the Mongol customary law attributed to Genghis Khan, but the progressive Islamisation of the western khanate brought in elements of Islamic law that conflicted with the Yasa's provisions, and this was one of the central political tensions of the fourteenth century. Kebek Khan (r. c. 1318–1326) tried to establish a settled seat of government near Nasaf, at the palace that gave the city of Qarshi its name. Together with his administrative division of Transoxiana into districts and his currency reform, this was the most serious attempt to turn the khanate from a nomadic confederation into a territorial state with consistent administrative capacity, but his successors lacked the will or the means to continue it. The khanate never reconciled the nomadic eastern tribes, whose pastoral traditions and largely shamanist and Buddhist religious practices were threatened by Islamisation and sedentarisation, with the urban commercial class of Transoxiana, whose prosperity required exactly the stable, Islam-friendly government that the eastern tribes rejected.
fields.impact: The Chagatai Khanate's historical impact was largely indirect, and came through the successor states it made possible rather than through its own institutions. Its most consequential contribution was unintended. The political and military world of the Chagataid domains produced Timur (Tamerlane, 1336–1405), a member of the Turkicised Barlas tribe, who built the Timurid Empire, the most powerful state of the late fourteenth- and fifteenth-century Islamic world. Under Timur and his successors, among them the astronomer-prince Ulugh Beg, its capital at Samarkand became one of the great centres of Islamic art, architecture and scholarship. The Chagataid dynastic line, used by Timur as a legitimising figurehead, continued to confer political legitimacy in Central Asia long after the khanate's effective dissolution. Babur, founder of the Mughal Empire in India (1526), was a Timurid on his father's side and a descendant of the Chagataid khans through his mother, so the Chagatai inheritance passed into one of the most consequential lines of descent in Asian imperial history. The khanate also gave its name to Chagatai Turkic, the literary language of Central Asia in which Ali-Shir Nava'i wrote his poetry and Babur his memoirs. The Silk Road commerce that the khanate taxed during its period of effective control formed part of the transcontinental exchange of goods, technologies and ideas characteristic of the Pax Mongolica era. These were also the routes along which, it is widely believed, the plague that became the Black Death spread westward. The khanate's Islamisation, culminating in Tarmashirin's conversion and confirmed in the east by Tughlugh Timur's conversion around 1354, helped fix the religious character of Central Asia as a Muslim region, with deep and long-lasting consequences from Afghanistan to the Tarim Basin.
fields.decline: The Chagatai Khanate declined unusually slowly, over nearly two centuries, through the progressive loss of governing capacity rather than through foreign conquest or sudden collapse. The khanate never built institutions able to survive the loss of any particular khan. Its government depended on the personal authority of the ruler and the temporary alignment of tribal interests. Khans succeeded one another rapidly, a sign of the violent politics of the nomadic confederation and of the inability of any individual ruler to create institutions that would outlast him. The final break came along the religious division that Tarmashirin's conversion exposed. His promotion of Islam and his shift of the political centre to the sedentary cities of Transoxiana alienated the eastern nomadic tribes to the point of revolt in 1334, and his overthrow and death opened a period in which the western khanate fell under the control of tribal amirs, above all Qazaghan, who killed the khan Qazan in 1346–1347 and ruled through puppet khans. Tughlugh Timur, raised to power in the east by the Dughlat, briefly reunited the khanate in 1360–1361, but Timur's seizure of Transoxiana in the following decade removed the khanate's economically vital western half for good. Only Moghulistan, the eastern rump based on the Ili valley steppe and the Tarim Basin, was left as a surviving Chagataid state. Moghulistan lasted in this diminished form for more than a century, its khans often dominated by the Dughlat amirs, and withstood Timurid invasions from the west and Oirat raids from the north-east. In the late fifteenth century it split between rival khans and gave way to a separate eastern khanate based at Turpan and to the Yarkent Khanate founded in 1514. The Chagataid line itself survived in these successors until their absorption by the Dzungars in the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries. As an independent governing entity, however, the khanate that had once commanded the central Silk Road from the Amu Darya to the Altai had dissolved into its nomadic and sedentary parts.
fields.summary: The Chagatai Khanate never settled whether it was a nomadic confederation or a sedentary state. The tension between steppe pastoral tradition and the Silk Road urban civilisation it governed produced the religious and cultural divisions along which it repeatedly fractured. It is a clear example of how Mongol successor states were changed and in the end absorbed by the societies they had conquered.
fields.teaser: The Chagatai Khanate, the Central Asian realm allotted to Genghis Khan's second son, Chagatai, ruled the lands between the Oxus and the Tarim Basin, gradually becoming Muslim and Turkic in culture.
fields.t0: The Mongol realm that Genghis Khan allotted to his son Chagatai, spanning Central Asia's steppe and Silk Road cities.
fields.t1: It produced Timur and, through him, a Chagataid line that helped legitimise the Mughal emperors of India.
fields.t2: Torn between nomadic tribes and settled Muslim cities, it split apart, losing Transoxiana to Timur by 1370.
fields.dyk: The city of Qarshi in Uzbekistan takes its name from the palace that Kebek Khan built there, near Nasaf, in the early 14th century.
